1.name: J.T. Rhoads
1.headline: A franchise-caliber passing foundation
1.bio: Rhoads gives a quarterback-needy team a strong case to stop searching. His fictional final season pairs 3,918 passing yards and 38 touchdowns with six interceptions. A 9.86 adjusted net yards-per-attempt mark captures that combination of explosive gains and controlled mistakes. Anticipation, coverage recognition and accuracy between the numbers lead the evaluation. The appeal at No. 1 is command of the whole passing game, rather than one spectacular throw. He changes launch points when needed and stays connected to his receivers' timing. The remaining work is handling late pressure without speeding up his lower body; the projection is a quarterback an offense can be built around.
1.watch: Keep his base settled against interior pressure and maintain timing when the first window closes.

2.name: Jaquon Hall
2.headline: A quarterback who changes the math for a defense
2.bio: Hall's fictional production combines 3,264 passing yards and 29 passing touchdowns with 924 rushing yards and 12 scores on the ground. That gives his Alabama profile a credible answer when defenses win the initial coverage matchup. He threatens the edge, resets to throw and can turn a conservative call into an explosive gain. His passing efficiency keeps the No. 2 projection from depending entirely on running ability. The next step is taking the available pocket completion more consistently instead of inviting extra contact while searching for something bigger.
2.watch: Stay ahead of pressure with the ball, preserve throwing rhythm and reduce unnecessary hits.

3.headline: An early pick who can change the front
3.bio: Williams' fictional Georgia season pairs 61 pressures on 342 rushes with 14.5 sacks and 22 tackles for loss. The 17.8% pressure rate gives the No. 3 projection substance beyond a strong frame or a few clean finishes. He can drive an offensive tackle backward, separate after contact and still affect the play when the quarterback avoids the initial rush. Thirty-three run stops add value on ordinary downs. At age 21, he projects as a defensive centerpiece, with the next step being quicker counters when protection commits extra attention to his first move.
3.watch: Develop quicker counters against extra protection and maintain rush-lane control when the first collision wins.
3.name: Cardarion Williams

6.name: Aaron Archuelta
6.headline: An early pick with a legitimate vertical ceiling
6.bio: Archuelta's fictional Penn State season produced 3,758 passing yards and 34 touchdowns, giving substance to a profile built around driving the ball outside the numbers and attacking deeper windows. His size helps him work over traffic, and his downfield ambition can force a defense to protect more grass. At No. 6, the draw is a potential offensive centerpiece with room to sharpen his efficiency. Ten interceptions leave a clear teaching point: improve touch underneath and recognize when a contested deep throw is an unnecessary bet.
6.watch: Layer intermediate throws, vary ball speed and take the underneath answer when the deep window disappears.

8.headline: Size and finish worthy of an early pick
8.bio: Pukahi's fictional Ohio State season includes 786 offensive snaps and an 84.8% run-block win rate. His 6-foot-8, 338-pound frame gives an offense a substantial edge to run behind, and his ability to displace a defender makes the size productive. Fourteen pressures allowed on 398 pass-blocking snaps leave a credible protection foundation alongside the rushing value. At No. 8, the projection is an immediate starting tackle with room to anchor a line for years. He still needs to keep his hips settled and avoid overcommitting when a rusher threatens inside.
8.watch: Stay balanced against inside counters and keep his recovery steps compact when the first punch misses.
8.name: Nakana'ela Pukahi

9.headline: A heavy edge with first-round disruption
9.bio: Patrick's fictional Texas Tech season produced 54 pressures, 11 sacks and 18 tackles for loss. His 16.2% pressure rate across 334 rushes supports a projection built on creating movement through contact rather than waiting for an untouched path. At 299 pounds, he can give a front options from a wider alignment or closer to the interior. Thirty run stops reinforce the case for meaningful responsibility at No. 9. More consistent pad level through longer rushes would help him keep his strength useful after the initial clash.
9.watch: Keep his pad level controlled and sustain his rush when a blocker survives the first contact.
9.name: Braeden Patrick

10.headline: A clean pocket starts with his side of the line
10.bio: Fitzwilliam's fictional Iowa season shows seven pressures allowed across 420 pass-blocking snaps, a 1.7% rate, with no sacks charged to him. That supports an early starting projection built on patient sets, controlled hand placement and the ability to stay connected without lunging. He gives a passing offense a dependable starting point at No. 10. His run-blocking contribution is useful, but the next step is creating more movement against heavier fronts rather than settling for a stalemate. The protection floor is the strongest part of a well-developed tackle profile.
10.watch: Create more displacement in the run game while preserving his patience and balance in protection.
10.name: Garrison Fitzwilliam

11.name: Narquise Jones
11.headline: A first-round receiver who can tilt the coverage
11.bio: Jones brings a fictional Minnesota season of 78 catches, 1,316 yards and 14 touchdowns to a profile with genuine lead-receiver ambition. His 3.23 yards per route run across 408 routes gives the No. 11 placement more substance than a handful of long catches. He can threaten a corner vertically, alter his pace into the break and create room for the rest of the passing game. The appeal is explosive production with enough route efficiency to project a substantial target share. The next step is keeping his releases clean against more patient, physical press coverage.
11.watch: Defeat patient press coverage and preserve route timing when the release gets crowded.

13.headline: A first-round matchup problem through the middle
13.bio: Zakrzewski's fictional Penn State season pairs 67 catches, 986 yards and 11 touchdowns with 3.02 yards per route run. That is meaningful receiving efficiency for a tight end, not simply the benefit of a few uncovered throws. He can threaten the seam, find space behind linebackers and give the quarterback an answer when outside receivers draw extra attention. At No. 13, the projection is a featured receiving piece with the production to justify early targets. His next step is firmer hand placement and more consistent leverage when asked to stay attached to the formation.
13.watch: Improve hand placement and sustain leverage as an inline run blocker without losing his receiving flexibility.
13.name: Aleks Zakrzewski

14.name: Nick Gardiner
14.headline: A polished distributor with a starter's pathway
14.bio: Gardiner's fictional final season features 3,551 passing yards, 28 touchdowns and eight interceptions. His appeal is the way those numbers fit a controlled passing game: quick identification, anticipation into intermediate windows and a willingness to keep the offense on schedule. The No. 14 placement reflects a strong starting projection without requiring every snap to become an improvisational showcase. He is comfortable directing traffic before the snap. His growth area is creating a second answer when protection breaks down, especially when moving away from his preferred throwing platform.
14.watch: Maintain accuracy on a disrupted platform and create practical answers outside the initial structure.

15.headline: A first-round answer for a pass-heavy offense
15.bio: Martens allowed nine pressures on 398 pass-blocking snaps in his fictional Alabama season, including one sack. His 2.3% pressure rate reinforces a projection built on clean set angles, repeatable footwork and keeping his hands available when a defender changes the rush plan. At No. 15, he has a persuasive case for early starting work at right tackle. The remaining question is how much more he can give a rushing attack. More consistent pad level and a stronger finish would turn dependable positioning into greater movement at the point of contact.
15.watch: Improve pad level and sustain his run blocks through the finish without losing protection discipline.
15.name: J.C. Martens

17.name: Nick Monk
17.headline: Get him the ball and let the yards follow
17.bio: Monk's fictional Florida State season produced 88 catches, 1,148 yards and 10 touchdowns, with 662 yards coming after the catch. Those 7.52 yards after catch per reception give a first-round evaluation meaningful support beyond the initial catch. He can find space underneath, turn upfield quickly and give an offense a credible manufactured-touch option without making that his entire role. At No. 17, the projection is a prominent target with room to become more complete. Finishing through contact and expanding his answers against outside press coverage remain useful next steps.
17.watch: Strengthen catch-point consistency through contact and develop more outside-release counters.

18.name: Francis Smith
18.headline: An early-down engine with first-round substance
18.bio: Smith's fictional Ohio State season delivered 1,438 rushing yards and 18 touchdowns on 238 carries. His 3.45 rushing yards after contact per carry reinforce the core appeal: he can stay on track through traffic, run behind his pads and finish gains after the blocking stops doing the work. The 225-pound frame supports a substantial workload, while 32 catches give the profile more flexibility than a pure handoff role. At No. 18, the expectation is meaningful offensive volume. The next step is making his protection recognition as dependable as his work between the tackles.
18.watch: Sharpen protection assignments and stay patient when the first interior lane is crowded.

19.headline: A strong edge for an offense that wants to run
19.bio: Ellis' fictional Penn State season features 774 offensive snaps and an 83.9% run-block win rate. He can generate movement on the edge, keep a defender occupied through contact and help an offense make its intended rushing lane usable. Eighteen pressures allowed across 426 pass-blocking snaps suggest a workable starting foundation, with technique still worth sharpening. At No. 19, his rushing contribution should translate into early responsibility. More patient hands and cleaner responses to late changes of direction would make the protection side of his game more dependable.
19.watch: Keep his feet active after contact and improve the timing of his hands against changing rush angles.
19.name: Cody Ellis

20.headline: A young tackle with real movement at the line
20.bio: Falana's fictional Auburn season produced 309 run-block wins on 365 assignments, an 84.7% rate. He can move a defender off the intended path and has the mass to help finish a rushing play once contact is established. At age 21 and No. 20 on the board, the run-game foundation comes with meaningful development time. Protection is the clearer teaching priority: 22 pressures on 408 pass-blocking snaps show where his technique must catch up. Better set depth and more controlled recovery steps would help him avoid chasing a rusher after losing the initial angle.
20.watch: Refine set depth and recover with his feet instead of reaching when the edge gets threatened.
20.name: Salene Falana

21.name: Chandu Chukwumerejie
21.headline: A sturdy target with first-round offensive utility
21.bio: Chukwumerejie's fictional Oklahoma season combines 75 catches, 1,089 yards and 11 touchdowns with 489 yards after the catch. The 213-pound build and productive work after the reception give him a credible path to a large role in the middle of a passing game. He can carry momentum through contact and give the quarterback a substantial target without needing every throw perfectly placed. At No. 21, the next layer is sharper route pacing: sell the vertical stem, separate earlier and avoid letting defenders settle on his intended break.
21.watch: Add deception to route stems and create cleaner separation before contact becomes necessary.

24.name: Jaylan Matthews Jr.
24.headline: A first-round creator who can manufacture extra yards
24.bio: Matthews turns a modest crease into a difficult tackling assignment. His fictional Alabama production includes 1,286 rushing yards, 14 rushing touchdowns and 41 receptions, giving the No. 24 projection a strong combination of rushing efficiency and passing-game involvement. Sixty-seven forced missed tackles add context to the appeal: the movement is productive when he gets a defender isolated. His compact build and changes of direction fit a prominent offensive role. He still needs to cut out unnecessary lateral steps when a direct gain is already available.
24.watch: Trust the first useful lane and improve consistency picking up pressure from the edge.

25.headline: A young edge with a clear path to passing-down impact
25.bio: White's fictional LSU season includes 46 pressures on 313 rushes, a 14.7% rate, with 9.5 sacks. His movement around the edge gives a defense a credible way to challenge protection without relying on an extra rusher. At age 21 and No. 25, there is room to grow into a larger role as his hand usage becomes more deliberate. The run-game contribution is less established: 18 stops and seven missed tackles leave a practical teaching priority. He needs to stay connected to his assignment when an offense runs toward him.
25.watch: Improve his contact balance against the run and connect his initial rush to a reliable counter.
25.name: Keshawn White

26.headline: A passing-game weapon worth moving around
26.bio: James' fictional Duke season produced 58 catches for 812 yards and nine touchdowns, including 348 yards after the catch. His 2.40 yards per route run supports a first-round projection built on getting him into useful space and letting him attack it. He can work across the formation, challenge intermediate coverage and turn a completed pass into another tackling problem. At No. 26, there is a clear path to early receiving work. His lighter frame and uneven run-blocking results make a full-time inline assignment less convincing until his leverage and contact timing improve.
26.watch: Build a more dependable blocking base and preserve route timing when defenders disrupt his release.
26.name: Nasir James Jr.

27.headline: A first-round edge with pressure and run-game utility
27.bio: Robinson's fictional NC State season features 45 pressures, nine sacks and 15 tackles for loss. His 14.1% pressure rate across 319 rushes gives the No. 27 placement a useful combination of disruption and repeatable work through contact. He can attack a tackle's set, force a reaction and finish when the quarterback holds the ball. Twenty-four run stops keep the projection broader than a narrow rush package. He still needs more variation once a blocker recognizes his preferred approach, particularly when the initial strike does not create separation.
27.watch: Vary his hand sequencing and respond sooner when the blocker sits on his first approach.
27.name: Deacon Robinson

28.headline: An imposing tackle with a starting pathway to refine
28.bio: Howard's fictional Texas A&M season combines 733 offensive snaps with an 80.8% run-block win rate. His 6-foot-8 frame gives him room to control the edge, and he can turn initial contact into useful movement when his pad level stays under control. The No. 28 projection is promising rather than finished. Twenty-four pressures and four sacks allowed across 431 pass-blocking snaps highlight the cost of standing too tall or opening the corner early. A team can build toward a starting role by sharpening his balance before asking his size to solve everything.
28.watch: Keep his pad level controlled and avoid opening his hips before the rusher commits.
28.name: Jamarcus Howard

30.name: Tye Miller
30.headline: A productive runner with room to broaden his role
30.bio: Miller's fictional Missouri season brings 1,278 rushing yards and 12 touchdowns on 221 carries to the evaluation. His pacing and one-cut decisions give him a credible path to sustained carries, and he can make a defender miss without turning every run into a long detour. The No. 30 placement reflects a strong rushing foundation with another layer still to develop. Twenty-four catches show some involvement through the air, but a wider receiving menu and more reliable protection would make his weekly role harder to take away.
30.watch: Expand his route detail and keep his feet disciplined when the intended lane closes.

31.headline: A starting pathway with another rush answer to develop
31.bio: Smith's fictional Wisconsin season delivered 43 pressures on 326 rushes, along with 8.5 sacks and 23 run stops. The production gives him a credible first-round foundation at No. 31, especially when he establishes contact on his terms and keeps the edge from opening cheaply. His 13.2% pressure rate is encouraging without suggesting every matchup is already solved. More precise hand placement and a quicker response after the first move stalls would help him become a more complete threat. The projection is early rotational value with a realistic route toward starting responsibility.
31.watch: Add a quicker counter and keep his hands accurate when the offensive tackle changes the contact point.
31.name: Hezekiah Smith

33.name: Kerry Williams Jr.
33.headline: A vertical weapon with a larger route tree to build
33.bio: Williams' fictional Texas season of 52 catches, 947 yards and nine touchdowns makes his downfield value easy to understand. His length gives him room to develop along the boundary, and the yards per catch fit a receiver who can stretch coverage. The No. 33 placement also reflects the unfinished work: only 52 of 91 targets became completions, and a lean 194-pound frame can make a clean release more important. He projects first as a complementary outside threat. Better functional strength and a more varied short-to-intermediate game would raise his ceiling.
33.watch: Build strength against press coverage, improve release variety and broaden his route inventory.

35.headline: Useful edge pressure with a lighter initial role
35.bio: Lake's fictional Oregon season produced 37 pressures and eight sacks across 297 rushes. His 12.5% pressure rate gives a passing-down package something useful to build around, particularly when he can challenge the outside angle before the tackle settles. At No. 35, the path to a larger role depends on the less glamorous work. Fourteen run stops and eight missed tackles show why he needs better control through contact. He must stay useful when an offense refuses the obvious passing situation instead of letting his rush assignment define every snap.
35.watch: Improve his run fits and tackling control, then add a dependable answer when the edge closes.
35.name: Desmond Lake

36.headline: An edge rotation piece with room to sharpen the finish
36.bio: Maldanado's fictional Ohio State season includes 38 pressures on 302 rushes, seven sacks and 22 run stops. He can challenge a block through contact and remain involved when a run stays near his side of the formation. That gives the No. 36 projection a broader foundation than a rush-only assignment. The next layer is turning early disruption into a cleaner finish: he needs more deliberate counters and better timing separating from the blocker. A rotational role is a reasonable opening, with larger responsibility tied to more consistent pressure and finishing.
36.watch: Time his separation more effectively and develop a clearer second move after initial contact.
36.name: Ricky Maldanado

37.headline: Useful movement with protection details to sharpen
37.bio: Smith's fictional Louisville season includes a 76.6% run-block win rate across 320 assignments. He can work across a defender's path, stay involved on combination blocks and help a rushing scheme create space through positioning. At No. 37, that movement gives him a practical starting point, while 27 pressures allowed on 443 pass-blocking snaps leave a clear development assignment. He needs a firmer response when contact lands squarely and more consistent hand placement after the initial set. The route to a larger role is cleaner technique against defenders who can challenge his balance.
37.watch: Strengthen his anchor and maintain hand position when the rush changes from movement to direct contact.
37.name: Darell Smith

38.headline: Interior disruption with development time on his side
38.bio: Crawford's fictional Clemson season produced 31 pressures on 288 rushes, a 10.8% rate from the interior, with 5.5 sacks. Those figures give his No. 38 projection a useful source of value: affecting the quarterback without requiring an untouched edge. Twenty-four run stops add evidence that he can remain involved beyond selected passing downs. At age 21, his next step is making his first contact more controlled and staying square when a blocker redirects him. The early role is a meaningful interior rotation, with room to grow into a more complete contributor.
38.watch: Keep his pad level controlled and avoid losing his run responsibility while searching for an interior opening.
38.name: Bobbie Crawford

39.headline: An interior run defender with a defined early role
39.bio: Francisco's fictional Oregon season features 30 run stops on 306 run-defense snaps, a 9.8% rate, with three missed tackles. That provides a practical reason to involve him in the middle of a front even when the sack total is modest. He can occupy space, resist the initial movement and help keep an intended running lane from opening cleanly. At No. 39, his 17 pressures and 2.5 sacks leave a less developed passing-down case. More effective separation after contact would expand his usefulness when the offense shifts away from the run.
39.watch: Separate from blocks more efficiently and develop a more productive passing-down response after first contact.
39.name: Johnathan Francisco

41.headline: A rotational rusher with a broader role to earn
41.bio: Robinson's fictional Missouri season includes 34 pressures on 286 rushes and 6.5 sacks. His 11.9% pressure rate gives a defense a workable reason to introduce him in selected situations, especially when his movement makes the blocker commit early. At No. 41, the challenge is becoming useful when those favorable rush conditions disappear. Fifteen run stops and seven missed tackles leave room to improve his positioning and control through contact. Better discipline at the edge and a more organized counter plan would make a larger workload easier to justify.
41.watch: Hold his edge assignment against the run and connect his initial movement to a more reliable counter.
41.name: Jahmiah Robinson

43.name: De'Quan Coleman
43.headline: A physical rotation back with a clear early role
43.bio: Coleman's fictional Colorado line of 1,167 rushing yards and 13 touchdowns supports a practical role in a rushing rotation. His 724 rushing yards after contact are the standout detail, pointing to a runner who can finish through contact and remain useful when space gets tight. At No. 43, his physical contribution is easier to project than a complete passing-down role. Seventeen catches leave that part of the profile less established. He needs cleaner transitions out of the backfield and better answers when a run asks him to redirect before building momentum.
43.watch: Improve receiving transitions and lateral resets without losing forward momentum.

44.headline: Useful early snaps, with a more defined ceiling
44.bio: Morgan-Stewart's fictional South Carolina line of 50 catches, 576 yards and six touchdowns points toward a useful complementary target. He works underneath, presents a large window and converted 14 of 24 contested targets in the authored season. A 74.2% run-block win rate adds a practical reason to keep him involved beyond passing situations. At No. 44, the value is a role that can be defined early. His 1.79 yards per route run and age-25 entry make a developmental-star projection harder to support; sharper transitions would help him create more than a safe outlet.
44.watch: Tighten transitions out of breaks and create separation before contested catches become the only answer.
44.name: Tyler Morgan-Stewart

45.headline: A young interior contributor with a stronger rushing-down case
45.bio: Browning's fictional Michigan season produced 28 run stops on 296 run-defense snaps, a 9.5% rate. He can keep contact useful in the middle, reduce space and help teammates reach a run before it develops into a clean lane. At age 21 and No. 45, that offers a practical foundation for rotational work. His passing-down contribution is less established: 19 pressures and three sacks across 227 rushes. Improving his separation timing and giving the blocker more than one problem after contact would help expand his role beyond the clearest rushing situations.
45.watch: Improve his separation timing and develop a more effective second action when his initial rush is contained.
45.name: Justice Browning

46.headline: A reliable run-game assignment with limited rush impact
46.bio: Schafer's fictional Duke season includes 29 run stops, 57 tackles and three missed tackles. The resulting 5.0% missed-tackle rate gives his No. 46 profile useful support as a defender who can turn correct positioning into a completed play. He can help control an edge and keep an offense from turning ordinary rushing calls into easy gains. The growth area is pressure: 24 disruptions and four sacks across 248 rushes suggest a supporting contribution. A sharper counter after his initial contact would make his role less dependent on the offense's run tendency.
46.watch: Add a more effective counter after first contact while maintaining his dependable run-game positioning.
46.name: Sam Schafer

48.headline: A workable receiving role with separation still to develop
48.bio: McFarland's fictional Alabama season includes 46 catches, 529 yards and five touchdowns. He can settle into underneath windows and offer a substantial target, but 1.66 yards per route run suggests supporting production rather than a ready-made focal point. His run-blocking results give him a chance to contribute to a rotation while the receiving details develop. At No. 48, the appeal is useful size and a manageable initial assignment. Better release variety and more decisive breaks against man coverage would help him turn those opportunities into a larger target share.
48.watch: Vary his releases, finish route breaks with conviction and sustain blocks through the end of the play.
48.name: Nik McFarland

49.headline: Interior movement with a starting job still to earn
49.bio: McCue's fictional Syracuse season features 250 run-block wins on 311 assignments, an 80.4% rate. His size and ability to create movement give him a defined way to contribute in the middle of a rushing attack. The No. 49 placement also leaves room for the protection work: 26 pressures allowed on 417 pass-blocking snaps show that his base and reactions are not yet equally dependable. He can compete for meaningful guard snaps, but quicker recognition of interior movement and more controlled lateral steps would make a sustained starting role easier to trust.
49.watch: Recognize interior exchanges earlier and keep his base controlled when a defender crosses his face.
49.name: Jeramy McCue

54.headline: Contact value with more consistency still to find
54.bio: Bailey's fictional Georgia season features 32 pressures on 284 rushes and six sacks. There are useful moments of disruption when he lands his initial contact and keeps the blocker reacting, but the 11.3% pressure rate supports a rotational projection at No. 54. Eighteen run stops and eight missed tackles leave additional work before a larger role becomes dependable. He needs to keep his feet active through the collision and avoid turning a promising position into an unfinished tackle. More consistent technique would help the useful flashes survive less favorable matchups.
54.watch: Keep his feet active through contact and improve tackle completion when the ball reaches his edge.
54.name: Kash Bailey

55.headline: Interior movement with a more complete role to develop
55.bio: Andrews' fictional Utah season produced 24 pressures on 256 rushes, with 4.5 sacks and 20 run stops. His interior movement can create a useful passing-down opportunity, but a 9.4% pressure rate still leaves a substantial difference between flashes and a dependable primary role. At No. 55, he should compete for a rotation while refining the details that keep him involved against the run. Better leverage through contact and a more controlled finish would help him avoid being redirected before the ball arrives. The next step is building a firmer foundation beneath the disruption.
55.watch: Improve leverage and contact balance so his interior movement does not come at the expense of his run responsibility.
55.name: Braylen Andrews

56.name: Nick Barrientos
56.headline: The throwing tools are ahead of the consistency
56.bio: Barrientos offers a developmental passing bet at No. 56. His fictional Miami line of 2,682 yards, 20 touchdowns and 12 interceptions shows both the vertical opportunity and the cost of uneven decisions. He can challenge distant windows, but the completion profile leaves too many routine plays unfinished. A team can build an early role around defined reads and selected deep shots while working on his base and release timing. The ceiling is useful; the case for immediate, every-down command of an offense still needs work.
56.watch: Improve short-area touch, repeat his footwork and separate an aggressive opportunity from a forced throw.

60.headline: A mobile interior option who needs a firmer base
60.bio: Baines' fictional Georgia season includes 711 offensive snaps and a 72.9% run-block win rate. He can reach space and help finish a combination block, giving a scheme that asks its guards to move a useful development candidate. Twenty-nine pressures allowed across 390 pass-blocking snaps make the protection concerns harder to overlook. At No. 60, a rotational role is the sensible opening rather than an automatic starting assignment. Better lower-body positioning and a more accurate first strike would help him avoid getting displaced before he can use his movement skills.
60.watch: Develop a firmer anchor and land his hands more consistently against direct interior pressure.
60.name: Darnell Baines

61.name: Johnny Newman
61.headline: A large receiving target with separation work ahead
61.bio: Newman's fictional Notre Dame season yielded 54 catches for 722 yards and eight touchdowns. A 56.7% contested-catch rate on 30 such targets gives context to the appeal of a 6-foot-6 receiver, especially around the end zone. They also show why he needs more separation rather than relying on reach to rescue every window. At No. 61, his size supports a useful situational role, while his route transitions and release timing need refinement before a bigger target load makes sense. A team is buying defined receiving options and a development plan, not a finished lead receiver.
61.watch: Sink into breaks more efficiently and create earlier separation against tight man coverage.

62.headline: A sturdy run contribution with a narrower passing-down role
62.bio: Brothers' fictional Stanford season includes 29 run stops across 306 run-defense snaps, a 9.5% rate, with 55 tackles. His 298-pound frame can help a front keep the edge controlled when he stays square and maintains contact. That gives him a defined route into a rotation at No. 62. The pass-rush profile is less convincing: 19 pressures and three sacks over 216 rushes. He needs more urgency off the snap and more efficient separation once the blocker establishes contact. A useful run assignment should be the starting point, with broader work earned through those improvements.
62.watch: Separate from blocks sooner and improve the urgency of his first steps on passing downs.
62.name: Jonathan Brothers

63.name: Zac Williams
63.headline: A developmental passer with a narrower margin for error
63.bio: Williams' fictional Ohio State season yielded 2,857 passing yards and 22 touchdowns against 11 interceptions. There are throws worth developing, especially when he has a clean setup and a defined target, but the efficiency does not yet support a plug-and-play starting projection. At No. 63, the sensible plan is a competitive reserve role with opportunities to earn more. He needs better timing on routine concepts and quicker exits from covered reads. Turning occasional high-end throws into reliable possessions will determine how much room he has to rise.
63.watch: Clean up routine accuracy, accelerate covered-read decisions and avoid holding the ball into sacks.

65.headline: A substantial middle with quicker reactions to develop
65.bio: Shea's fictional Notre Dame season produced a 78.1% run-block win rate across 342 assignments. His 328-pound frame offers a useful base for controlling space in the middle, particularly when he can establish contact on schedule. The No. 65 projection becomes less certain when the protection speeds up: 28 pressures were allowed over 430 pass-blocking snaps. He needs cleaner foot placement against quick interior movement and more reliable transitions when helping a neighboring blocker. There is a workable reserve-center foundation, with a larger role dependent on steadier execution after the snap.
65.watch: React sooner to quick interior movement and transition cleanly between helping and taking over a defender.
65.name: Matt Shea

67.name: Qualeek Leonard
67.headline: Useful size and movement, with a workload to earn
67.bio: Leonard's fictional Notre Dame season produced 828 rushing yards and seven touchdowns on 156 carries. The efficiency gives him something to build on, but the smaller workload makes a featured-back projection premature. He can redirect for a larger runner, and his 230-pound frame offers options in a rotation. At No. 67, he is a development candidate who should earn touches before being handed a full role. More decisive reads through congested lanes and a stronger passing-down contribution would help turn those opportunities into a lasting job.
67.watch: Make quicker interior decisions and improve protection reliability before expanding his workload.

70.headline: A developmental edge with a rush plan to sharpen
70.bio: Nyokare's fictional UConn season includes 28 pressures on 272 rushes and 5.5 sacks. His movement creates opportunities to attack an outside angle, but a 10.3% pressure rate does not yet establish a dependable featured role. At No. 70, he is a development candidate who needs a clearer answer when the initial path closes. Fourteen run stops and eight missed tackles add a second priority: becoming more controlled when the play comes toward him. Better hand sequencing and a firmer response through contact would help turn selected rush opportunities into a lasting job.
70.watch: Build a more organized counter plan and improve his ability to finish tackles through contact.
70.name: Kaziri Nyokare

71.headline: A reserve-center pathway with finishing work ahead
71.bio: Bauer's fictional Michigan season features 753 offensive snaps, with 23 pressures allowed across 367 pass-blocking assignments. There are useful moments of patience and positioning in that protection profile, but a 69.9% run-block win rate makes consistent movement a clear development need. At No. 71, he is a candidate to compete for reserve-center work and earn more through technique. He must keep his base intact after the initial strike and sustain control when a defender resists the intended path. Reliable execution on ordinary interior assignments will matter more than occasional clean reps in space.
71.watch: Sustain control after first contact and improve the consistency of his run-block finish.
71.name: Jacob Bauer

72.headline: A young rush option with a dependable floor to build
72.bio: Thompson's fictional Clemson season produced 26 pressures and five sacks on 251 rushes. At age 21, he has time to make his movement more productive, but the 10.4% pressure rate supports a developmental projection at No. 72. He needs better timing between his first steps and his hands so a promising rush does not end in a controlled stalemate. Sixteen run stops and seven missed tackles show why a narrow package should come before a substantial workload. More disciplined positioning would help him remain useful when the offense chooses to attack his side.
72.watch: Coordinate his hands with his first steps and improve run positioning before expanding his workload.
72.name: Shad Thompson

73.headline: A tall tackle with a substantial technique assignment
73.bio: Wilkins' fictional Charlotte season includes 692 offensive snaps, but 37 pressures and five sacks allowed across 404 pass-blocking assignments point to a developmental protection profile. His 6-foot-7 frame gives a coach something to work with; it does not yet guarantee a clean edge. At age 21 and No. 73, the reasonable plan is competitive depth with deliberate work on set angles and recovery. A 69.8% run-block win rate also leaves room to improve leverage. He needs more control before his size can translate into dependable starting snaps.
73.watch: Improve set angles, lower his pad level and recover without reaching after losing position.
73.name: Jaden Wilkins

74.headline: Downfield options to develop, routine details to fix
74.bio: Jackson's fictional LSU season produced 31 catches for 432 yards and five touchdowns. His 13.94 yards per reception offers a reason to explore selected seam and downfield assignments, but only 31 of 58 targets became completions. At No. 74, the receiving outline is more promising than its consistency. His size can create opportunities, yet he needs cleaner releases, more reliable ball tracking and better timing into the catch point. A limited package is a reasonable starting role while he works toward becoming a dependable option on ordinary downs.
74.watch: Improve ball tracking and release timing, then broaden the routes he can execute reliably.
74.name: Theodore Jackson Jr.

75.headline: A passing-down opportunity that still needs a finish
75.bio: Jennings' fictional South Carolina season yielded 23 pressures and four sacks across 239 rushes. He can make an offensive tackle respond to the outside path, but the 9.6% pressure rate leaves room to turn that initial reaction into more meaningful disruption. At No. 75, the sensible starting point is a selected rush package and a competition for reserve snaps. Ten run stops and seven missed tackles make a large early workload harder to support. He needs stronger contact balance, cleaner finishing and a more dependable counter when the edge is protected.
75.watch: Improve contact balance and develop a reliable second action when his first rush path is closed.
75.name: Jaquann Jennings

76.headline: Rushing value with protection that needs to catch up
76.bio: Davison's fictional Ole Miss season shows a 78.2% run-block win rate, giving his 332-pound frame a practical role in creating rushing space. The protection results are less settled: 39 pressures and six sacks allowed across 427 pass-blocking snaps. At No. 76, he should compete for a defined backup role while improving his set discipline. He can remain useful when a play lets him establish contact early, but quicker edge threats expose the need for better positioning. The next step is making his feet reliable enough to keep the quarterback from inheriting the recovery problem.
76.watch: Improve set discipline against the edge and stay connected when a defender avoids his initial contact.
76.name: Dee Davison

77.headline: A rotational guard with interior pressure to clean up
77.bio: Lee's fictional Ole Miss season pairs a 77.3% run-block win rate with 36 pressures allowed on 419 pass-blocking snaps. His frame and ability to create movement give him a route into a rushing rotation, but the 8.6% pressure rate limits the case for immediate starting trust. At No. 77, the priority is improving the details that keep an interior pocket usable. He needs earlier recognition of moving fronts, a more consistent strike and better balance when passing a defender between blockers. Those improvements would make his run-game contribution easier to keep on the field.
77.watch: Identify interior exchanges sooner and keep his feet and hands coordinated when the front shifts.
77.name: Brandon Lee

79.headline: Movement potential with a dependable floor still to build
79.bio: Fisher's fictional Tennessee season produced 715 offensive snaps and a 71.1% run-block win rate. His movement gives him opportunities on plays that change the blocking angle, but 39 pressures allowed across 431 pass-blocking assignments show how much consistency remains to develop. At No. 79, he is better viewed as competitive tackle depth than a ready-made starting answer. He must improve the accuracy of his first strike, avoid crossing his feet during recovery and sustain blocks after reaching the right spot. Getting into position is useful only if he can stay effective there.
79.watch: Improve first-contact accuracy, keep recovery steps controlled and sustain blocks beyond initial positioning.
79.name: Colt Fisher

80.headline: Interior depth with a defined rushing-down assignment
80.bio: Vanwinkle's fictional USC season includes 25 run stops across 289 run-defense snaps, an 8.7% rate. His 330-pound frame offers a reason to compete for work in the middle when the assignment is to resist movement and keep a running lane crowded. At No. 80, that is a more convincing opening than projecting substantial quarterback pressure. Eleven pressures and one sack across 184 rushes show how limited the passing-down contribution remains. Better pad level and quicker separation after contact would help him become more than a situational depth option.
80.watch: Keep his pad level controlled and develop a quicker way to separate once the blocker establishes contact.
80.name: Hugh Vanwinkle

83.name: Demond Henderson
83.headline: A rotational option who needs cleaner possessions
83.bio: Henderson's fictional North Carolina season offers 839 rushing yards and eight touchdowns, but four fumbles make ball security a central part of the evaluation. He has the build to handle contact and enough movement to compete for rotational carries. The No. 83 placement reflects the distance between those usable traits and a dependable expanded role. He needs to secure the ball through traffic, reach decisions sooner and get more from ordinary rushing opportunities. Until those details improve, a limited workload is a more reasonable starting point than featured usage.
83.watch: Protect the ball through contact, eliminate hesitation and earn trust on passing downs.

84.headline: A blocking role to earn before the target count grows
84.bio: Cook's fictional LSU receiving line is modest: 14 catches for 138 yards and one touchdown. The stronger case for a roster role comes from 154 run-block wins on 196 assignments, a 78.6% rate, with three pressures allowed across 58 pass-blocking snaps. His 264-pound frame fits a job helping an offense finish its blocking structure. At No. 84, that contribution matters more than forcing a high-volume receiving projection. He still needs cleaner releases and more dependable hands to keep defenses from treating his presence as an automatic run indicator.
84.watch: Develop cleaner releases and reliable short catches while maintaining his blocking contribution.
84.name: Daronte Cook

86.name: Jaylon Clarke
86.headline: Downfield size that still needs a dependable floor
86.bio: Clarke's fictional Iowa State season includes 39 catches, 684 yards and six touchdowns. The explosive average gives his 6-foot-4 frame a possible boundary role, but 39 completions on 76 targets make consistency a substantial part of the projection. At No. 86, he should begin as a selective vertical option rather than an automatic starter. He needs more purposeful releases, better timing locating the ball and a route tree that creates work when the deep shot is unavailable. The tools can earn an opportunity; the routine details will decide whether he keeps it.
86.watch: Improve ball tracking, tighten release timing and become useful on nonvertical routes.

89.name: Joseph Lomeli
89.headline: An underneath contributor with a limited initial projection
89.bio: Lomeli's fictional Boise State season produced 62 catches, 714 yards and four touchdowns. His 62 completions on 86 targets suggest a workable underneath connection, but the modest output across 421 routes points toward a supporting role. At No. 89, he can compete to keep possessions moving from inside alignments. He still needs to create more against tight man coverage, threaten defenders beyond the first break and turn short catches into more meaningful gains. The initial appeal is practical receiving depth; a larger role will require more separation and more explosive production.
89.watch: Generate separation against man coverage and add more value after short receptions.

92.name: Kiaan Brown
92.headline: Receiving value in a role that still needs definition
92.bio: Brown's fictional USC line includes 46 receptions for 472 yards and four receiving touchdowns, alongside 451 rushing yards on 96 carries. That passing-game involvement gives him an identifiable way onto the field at No. 92. He can work as an outlet and underneath option, but the rushing volume does not establish an every-down answer. His development priorities are practical: hold up in protection, add detail against tighter coverage and prove he can handle more carries without sacrificing efficiency. A targeted receiving package is the clearest initial projection.
92.watch: Improve protection, win routes beyond easy outlets and build evidence for a larger rushing role.

93.headline: A developmental guard with an anchor to strengthen
93.bio: Varela's fictional USC season includes 669 offensive snaps, but 43 pressures allowed on 411 pass-blocking assignments leave a substantial protection concern. His movement can help on selected assignments, yet a 67.4% run-block win rate shows that getting to a defender is not the same as controlling him. At No. 93, the starting point is a depth competition with significant technique work ahead. He needs a firmer anchor, better timing at contact and fewer penalties before a larger role is justified. Improving the routine interior reps will do more for his prospects than isolated flashes in space.
93.watch: Strengthen his anchor, improve strike timing and reduce penalties before taking on a larger workload.
93.name: Renaldo Varela

94.headline: A developmental receiving option with trust to build
94.bio: Whitney's fictional Oregon season includes 25 catches, 344 yards and three touchdowns. There are useful gains in that sample, but 25 completions on 49 targets and 1.32 yards per route run leave a significant gap between occasional impact and a dependable weekly role. At No. 94, he projects as competitive depth with selected receiving opportunities. His 259-pound frame gives him something to work with, but size alone will not secure snaps. He needs more precise route pacing, better adjustments to the ball and consistent execution on the shorter throws.
94.watch: Improve catch-point adjustments, sharpen route pacing and become dependable on routine underneath throws.
94.name: Brendan Whitney

95.headline: Reserve-edge competition with more impact to prove
95.bio: Whitt's fictional Michigan season features 39 tackles and 18 run stops, but 16 pressures and two sacks across 221 rushes leave a limited disruption profile. He can contribute a controlled fit when his initial positioning is correct, yet seven missed tackles show that reaching the play is not always enough. At No. 95, he should be evaluated as competitive reserve depth with specific technique work ahead. A firmer response to contact, more efficient separation and cleaner tackling would give him a stronger case when an offense refuses the most favorable assignment.
95.watch: Improve tackling through contact and separate from blocks more efficiently before seeking a larger role.
95.name: Denver Whitt

96.headline: A developmental edge who needs a more complete sequence
96.bio: McKinley's fictional Illinois season produced 18 pressures and three sacks on 246 rushes, a 7.3% pressure rate. His first contact can give a tackle something to manage, but too many rushes end before that moment becomes a meaningful threat to the quarterback. At No. 96, he needs a clearer second move and better control at the edge. Sixteen run stops and eight missed tackles reinforce the need for steadier execution. The starting projection is a depth competition, with a larger role dependent on connecting his approach, separation and finish.
96.watch: Connect his first contact to a useful counter and improve his control when finishing at the edge.
96.name: Jerrick McKinley
